questions.question: Define electric current.
questions.modelAnswer: The rate of flow of electric charge. Current = charge ÷ time.
markingPoints: The rate of flow of electric charge.
Current = charge ÷ time.

questions.question: Define potential difference.
questions.modelAnswer: Energy transferred per unit charge between two points. P.d. = energy ÷ charge.
markingPoints: Energy transferred per unit charge between two points.
P.d. = energy ÷ charge.

questions.question: Explain what resistance does in a circuit.
questions.modelAnswer: It opposes the flow of charge. For a given potential difference, greater resistance gives a smaller current.
markingPoints: It opposes the flow of charge.
For a given potential difference, greater resistance gives a smaller current.

questions.question: Describe the current–potential difference graph for an ohmic resistor at constant temperature.
questions.modelAnswer: A straight line through the origin. Current is directly proportional to potential difference. Resistance is constant.
markingPoints: A straight line through the origin.
Current is directly proportional to potential difference.
Resistance is constant.

questions.question: Explain why the resistance of a filament lamp increases as current increases.
questions.modelAnswer: The filament temperature rises. Ions vibrate more. Electrons collide more frequently, so resistance increases.
markingPoints: The filament temperature rises.
Ions vibrate more.
Electrons collide more frequently, so resistance increases.

questions.question: Describe the current–potential difference characteristic of a diode.
questions.modelAnswer: Very high resistance in the reverse direction. Little current flows until the forward threshold is reached. Then current rises steeply.
markingPoints: Very high resistance in the reverse direction.
Little current flows until the forward threshold is reached.
Then current rises steeply.

questions.question: State how the resistance of an NTC thermistor changes as temperature increases.
questions.modelAnswer: Its resistance decreases.
markingPoints: Its resistance decreases.

questions.question: State how the resistance of an LDR changes as light intensity increases.
questions.modelAnswer: Its resistance decreases.
markingPoints: Its resistance decreases.

questions.question: State the rules for current, potential difference and resistance in a series circuit.
questions.modelAnswer: Current is the same everywhere. Supply p.d. is shared. Total p.d. equals the sum across components. Total resistance is the sum of component resistances.
markingPoints: Current is the same everywhere.
Supply p.d. is shared.
Total p.d. equals the sum across components.
Total resistance is the sum of component resistances.

questions.question: State the rules for current and potential difference in a parallel circuit.
questions.modelAnswer: Potential difference is the same across each branch. Current splits at junctions. Total current equals the sum of branch currents. Adding branches reduces total resistance.
markingPoints: Potential difference is the same across each branch.
Current splits at junctions.
Total current equals the sum of branch currents.
Adding branches reduces total resistance.

questions.question: Explain why adding another resistor in parallel reduces total resistance.
questions.modelAnswer: It provides another path for charge. More total current flows for the same supply potential difference. Because R = V/I, total resistance decreases.
markingPoints: It provides another path for charge.
More total current flows for the same supply potential difference.
Because R = V/I, total resistance decreases.

questions.question: Distinguish direct current from alternating current.
questions.modelAnswer: Direct current flows in one direction. Alternating current repeatedly changes direction and magnitude.
markingPoints: Direct current flows in one direction.
Alternating current repeatedly changes direction and magnitude.

questions.question: State the frequency and potential difference of the UK mains supply.
questions.modelAnswer: 50 Hz and approximately 230 V.
markingPoints: 50 Hz and approximately 230 V.

questions.question: State the function and colour of the live, neutral and earth wires in a UK plug.
questions.modelAnswer: Live: brown, carries alternating p.d. from supply. Neutral: blue, completes the circuit and is near 0 V. Earth: green/yellow, safety wire connected to metal case and normally carries no current.
markingPoints: Live: brown, carries alternating p.d. from supply.
Neutral: blue, completes the circuit and is near 0 V.
Earth: green/yellow, safety wire connected to metal case and normally carries no current.

questions.question: Explain how the earth wire and fuse protect a person if the live wire touches a metal case.
questions.modelAnswer: The case becomes connected to earth through a low-resistance path. A large current flows. The fuse melts or circuit breaker opens. The live supply is disconnected, reducing electric-shock risk.
markingPoints: The case becomes connected to earth through a low-resistance path.
A large current flows.
The fuse melts or circuit breaker opens.
The live supply is disconnected, reducing electric-shock risk.

questions.question: Explain why the National Grid transmits electricity at high potential difference.
questions.modelAnswer: For the same power, a higher p.d. gives a lower current. Heating loss in cables depends on I²R. Lower current reduces energy wasted and improves efficiency.
markingPoints: For the same power, a higher p.d. gives a lower current.
Heating loss in cables depends on I²R.
Lower current reduces energy wasted and improves efficiency.

questions.question: Explain how rubbing two insulating materials can charge them.
questions.modelAnswer: Electrons transfer from one material to the other. The material gaining electrons becomes negative. The one losing electrons becomes positive. Protons do not move.
markingPoints: Electrons transfer from one material to the other.
The material gaining electrons becomes negative.
The one losing electrons becomes positive.
Protons do not move.

questions.question: Define an electric field and state its direction around a positive charge.
questions.modelAnswer: A region where a charged object experiences a force. Field direction is the direction of force on a positive test charge. It points away from a positive charge.
markingPoints: A region where a charged object experiences a force.
Field direction is the direction of force on a positive test charge.
It points away from a positive charge.

questions.question: A current of 0.40 A flows for 3.0 minutes. Calculate the charge transferred.
markingPoints: Q = It
Q = 72 C

questions.question: A resistor has a potential difference of 12 V and a current of 0.30 A. Calculate its resistance.
markingPoints: R = V ÷ I
R = 40 Ω

questions.question: A 2.0 kW heater is used for 15 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred in joules.
markingPoints: E = Pt

questions.question: A kettle operates at 230 V with a current of 10 A. Calculate its power.
markingPoints: P = VI

questions.question: A charge of 45 C passes through a component at 6.0 V. Calculate the energy transferred.
markingPoints: E = QV

questions.question: Describe how to obtain current–potential difference data for a resistor, filament lamp and diode.
questions.modelAnswer: Connect an ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel with the component. Use a variable resistor or variable supply. Change p.d. in steps and record V and I. Reverse the supply to obtain negative values where safe. Control the resistor’s temperature or allow cooling. Plot current against p.d.
markingPoints: Connect an ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel with the component.
Use a variable resistor or variable supply.
Change p.d. in steps and record V and I.
Reverse the supply to obtain negative values where safe.
Control the resistor’s temperature or allow cooling.
Plot current against p.d.

questions.question: Describe how to investigate how the resistance of a wire depends on its length.
questions.modelAnswer: Use one wire of uniform material and diameter. Connect ammeter in series and voltmeter across a measured length. Change length using a sliding contact, record V and I, and calculate R = V/I. Keep temperature low/constant by using small current and switching off between readings. Repeat and plot resistance against length.
markingPoints: Use one wire of uniform material and diameter.
Connect ammeter in series and voltmeter across a measured length.
Change length using a sliding contact, record V and I, and calculate R = V/I.
Keep temperature low/constant by using small current and switching off between readings.
Repeat and plot resistance against length.

questions.question: Three series resistors are 4 Ω, 7 Ω and 9 Ω. Calculate total resistance.
questions.modelAnswer: Rₜ = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ Rₜ = 4 + 7 + 9 Rₜ = 20 Ω
markingPoints: Rₜ = R₁ + R₂ + R₃
Rₜ = 20 Ω

questions.question: A resistor has resistance 15 Ω and carries 2.0 A. Calculate its power.
questions.modelAnswer: P = I²R P = 2.0² × 15 P = 60 W
markingPoints: P = I²R
P = 60 W
